description: University undergrads with an interest to explore earth science data analysis, real life application of coursework, to further broaden our expertise.
summary:
buzzball is a Streamlit app that asks two questions of NASA satellite and model data: what is changing, and should we worry? It covers Indonesia's peat-fire regions (Central Kalimantan, Riau / South Sumatra) and Singapore, where the smoke arrives. The data are monthly fire counts, haze (aerosol optical depth), air dryness, soil moisture, rainfall and temperature.

Every variable goes through four trend tests. These are seasonal Kendall, Mann-Kendall, a t-test adjusted for autocorrelation, and a regression that removes El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole swings. The results come back as plain-language verdicts. The app also flags unusual months, finds the dominant patterns, and measures how much of Singapore's haze comes from fires upwind.

For forecasting, it compares nine models, from simple baselines to gradient boosting and neural networks. Each model is tested by predicting past years from earlier data only, so no model sees the future. The app then recommends the most accurate model, or a simpler one that scores nearly as well. An animated globe maps fires and trends across the region. An AI-powered advisor suggests related variables, a forecast model and extra NASA datasets to add
details:
What it does
buzzball answers two questions about Earth observation data: what is changing, and should we worry? Our case study is Indonesia's peat fires and the haze they send to Singapore. It uses monthly NASA data from 2001 to 2025 for three regions: Central Kalimantan, Riau / South Sumatra, and Singapore.

How it works
A user picks a place, a concern (fires, haze, drying, heat or rain) and a range of years. The app then says in plain language whether the change is real or could be chance.

The verdict rests on four trend tests we wrote from scratch:

  • seasonal Kendall
  • Mann-Kendall
  • a t-test adjusted for autocorrelation
  • a regression that removes El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole effects

Other pages:

  • flag unusual months
  • find variables that move together
  • measure how closely Singapore's haze follows fires upwind
  • show a 3D globe with a year-by-year time-lapse and trend maps for each grid cell.

For forecasting, the app compares nine models, from seasonal averages to gradient boosting and a small neural network. Each model predicts every year from 2011 using only earlier data. The app recommends a model only if it beats the seasonal average.

Rule-based alerts can go to Slack or email, and an optional AI chat explains the results.

Benefits and impact
Haze agencies, health planners and researchers get an honest early read on fire-season risk without needing a statistician. Users can upload any monthly CSV, so the tool works for other regions and variables too.

Tools

  • Software: Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, xarray, Plotly and the Anthropic API, run on a laptop.
    • NASA FIRMS (MODIS active fires)
    • GPM IMERG (rainfall)
    • GLDAS-2.1 (soil moisture, temperature, evapotranspiration)
    • MERRA-2 (aerosol optical depth)
    • NOAA El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole indices

What is creative

  • Testing whether a trend is real. We ran standard tests on simulated data that had no trend but did have month-to-month carry-over. They wrongly found a trend in 29–30% of series. Our corrected tests kept this to 8–10%.
  • Models must earn their place. Three months ahead, ridge regression beat the seasonal average by 12–13% for fires in both hotspots. For rainfall and soil moisture no model did, and the app says so instead of showing a confident but useless forecast.
  • Fires linked to haze. It connects where fires burn to where the haze arrives.

Factors we considered

  • Seasons and El Niño can create false trends, so we remove both.
  • Fire counts before mid-2002 come from one satellite only, so the early record runs low.
  • GLDAS models mineral soil, not peat, so it shows only relative drying.
  • Correlation is not causation: people light most of these fires.
  • With 300 months of data, an LSTM would be too data-hungry.
  • The AI chat sees only computed summaries, never raw data, and everything except the chat works without an API key.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

We used SI tools in three places.

  1. Code and documentation. Claude Code (Anthropic's Claude, in VS Code) wrote and revised much of the Python code: the statistics, the model comparison, the app pages and the globe. It also ran the tests, fixed bugs, wrote the README and drafted this description. The team set the goals, reviewed the changes and checked the results in the running app.
  2. Design. Figma Make, Figma's AI prototyping tool, generated the dashboard design that the app's dark theme and Start page layout follow.
  3. Inside the app. The optional AI chat uses the Claude API to answer questions about the results. It receives only computed summaries, never raw data. The app's variable and model recommendations come from our own code, not from the AI.
